Before you start

Students learn what to say after hello: follow-up questions, going one layer deeper, and ending with a thread to pick up later, then practice for one minute in pairs. Nothing to bring; let anyone pass or pair with a friend, and keep it about skills, never about who in the room is quiet.

Every student in the room

Conversation styles differ by culture, language and neurotype, so treat eye contact, loudness and interrupting as styles, never as the right way (slides 2, 4 and the practice minute).

Slide 1 · Notes

Something like: adults take workshops on this. Nobody here needs fixing. A short, slightly embarrassing story of your own works well here.

Slide 2 · Notes

Take a few shout-outs. They usually land on: asks about you, remembers, doesn’t make it all about them. Nobody says “really clever.”

Slide 3 · Notes

Quick hands-up vote. The next slide shows what researchers found.

Slide 4 · Notes

Ask: “Why would a follow-up matter more than a first question?” It proves you were listening.

Slide 5 · Notes

Ask: “When does a shift work?” When they ask you back, or a quick “me too” and then back to them. Order matters.

Slide 6 · Notes

Most conversations stall at facts. One layer down is where it gets interesting.

Slide 7 · Notes

None of these is the right way. Follow-ups and trading turns work for quiet and loud, in any language.

Slide 8 · Notes

Time one minute each way. Then ask: how did it feel to only follow? To be asked? Usually weird to ask, nice to be asked.

Take a few guesses. The next slide shows the number.

Next time, open with the thread: “How’d the audition go?” That’s how one conversation becomes a second one.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students learn what keeps a conversation going after hello: follow-up questions, trading turns, going one layer deeper, and ending with a thread to pick up next time. They practice for one minute with a partner. Nobody is asked to become more outgoing.

Materials

  • Nothing required. Students pair up from where they sit.
  • Index cards or notebooks for the private closing question
  • The student page link (last slide) to share after advisory

Flow

  1. 2 minOpen: who's easy to talk to?
  2. 3 minQuestions make people like you
  3. 2 minShift or follow?
  4. 2 minThree layers, and trading turns
  5. 4 minThe follow-up minute (pairs)
  6. 2 minEnd with a thread
  7. 4 minThree moments
  8. 1 minOne person this week (private) and the student page

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Who's easy to talk to (2), Shift or follow (2), the follow-up minute in pairs (4), the student page link (2). The student page has the research and the rest of the moves.

Before you teach
Frame it as a skill everyone uses.

Say early that adults take workshops on this, and that nobody in the room needs fixing. Teens shut down fast if this sounds like a lesson for the kids who don't have friends.

Never single out the quiet students.

No "let's hear from someone we don't usually hear from." Some students are shy, some are thinking, some are tired. Quiet is a style.

Make the practice easy to say yes to.

Pairs can be friends. A trio is fine. Anyone can pass or just listen. Give a silly default topic (best and worst food in the cafeteria) so nobody has to share anything personal.

Expect some groans, and roll with it.

"This is so awkward" is the right answer. Agree: "It is. That's kind of the point. Everyone's a little awkward the first minute."

Watch for the student who's really struggling.

If a student says they never talk to anyone, avoids lunch, or seems lonely for a long time, check in privately afterward and walk them to a counselor that day. Social anxiety is common and treatable.

Use your own story.

A time you didn't know what to say (first day of a job, a party where you knew one person) does more than any slide.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Eye contact and directness are cultural.

In many families, looking an adult in the eye is rude, and asking personal questions early is intrusive. Present the moves as options and invite students to say how conversation works at their home.

Autistic and ADHD students.

Some students find these moves useful as a script, and some find small talk exhausting or pointless. Both are fair. Talking side by side (walking, gaming, building something) counts as conversation. Interrupting can be excitement; don't treat it as rudeness.

Students learning English, or with an accent.

Conversation in a second language is harder work. A follow-up question is easier than a clever comment, which is good news. Talking in their home language with friends counts too.

Students who stutter or have a speech difference.

The practice minute is optional and has no clock pressure on the person answering. Never finish a student's sentence.

Don't assume the answers.

Model questions that don't assume a family, money or a relationship: "What did you get up to this weekend?" instead of "Where'd you go on vacation?" or "Do you have a girlfriend?"

Some students are the only one.

A student who is one of few from their race, culture, or background may carry more of the work of starting conversations. Name that it can be harder, and that it's never their job alone to make others comfortable.

What the research says

In online chats and speed dates, people who asked more questions were liked more by their partners, and follow-up questions did most of the work. Speed daters who asked more follow-ups got more second dates.

Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson and Gino, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2017

People expected deeper conversations with strangers to feel more awkward and less enjoyable than they did, and underestimated how interested the other person would be in their answers.

Kardas, Kumar and Epley, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2022

Conversations almost never ended when both people wanted them to. In one study it was about 2% of conversations.

Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney and Wilson, PNAS, 2021

Strangers who took turns answering questions that got slowly more personal felt much closer after 45 minutes than pairs who made small talk.

Aron, Melinat, Aron, Vallone and Bator, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 1997

Sociologist Charles Derber described two kinds of reply: a shift response turns the talk back to you, a support response keeps it on the other person.

Derber, The Pursuit of Attention, 1979

People feel close to someone who seems to understand them and care about what they said. Researchers call it responsiveness.

Reis and Shaver, 1988; Reis and Clark, 2013

The Finding Your People lesson covers the long game: about 50 hours together to a casual friend, 200 to a close one, and the liking gap.

Hall, 2019; Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom and Clark, 2018
